opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the more important change wasn't the raw quantity. People like to ask, "How many more tokens did you train on?" or "How many more video clips?", as if that's the headline. Of course the volume went up quite a lot from the first model to the next generation. But if I had to sum it up, our view of what "more data" means changed.

With the first model, the main question was whether we had enough data, at enough scale, to get the model to work at all. We were collecting broadly and filtering fairly coarsely. Once we saw what the model could and couldn't do, we realized many of its failures weren't about too little data. They came from data that wasn't distributed well. Some domains, motions, or camera behaviors were overrepresented. Others, often the ones users actually cared about, were very thin.

So for the next generation, a big share of the effort went into curation rather than accumulation:
- better filtering and deduplication,
- better captions and annotations,
- deliberately rebalancing the mixture toward the long tail.

In some ways, the data we threw away mattered as much as the data we added.

The second thing I'd say is that the gains don't scale linearly. Early on, doubling the data gives you very visible improvements. Later, simply adding more of the same kind gives diminishing returns. The improvement comes from data that teaches the model something it didn't already know. That pushed us to think harder about data diversity and quality signals, and about how pretraining data interacts with what comes afterward, in post-training.

So my assessment is this. Yes, the increase was substantial and necessary; you can't skip scale. But the real lesson from the first model to the second was that scale is the entry ticket, not the differentiator. The differentiator is how well you understand your data: what's in it, what's missing, and what the model actually learns from it. That's where I think a lot of the remaining headroom still is.

r001.rationale: The response says the first model used coarser filtering and the next generation used better filtering, but it does not explain that this changed the first-generation baseline for measuring the data increase.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, the jump in pretraining data between our first model and the next generation was less about raw volume and more about what the data actually taught the model.

For the first version, we were honestly data-constrained. We used what we could gather, cleaned it reasonably well, and the scale was modest. When we started the next generation, the easy move was to just multiply the token count. We did scale up quite a bit, but what mattered more was the composition. We spent a lot of effort on filtering, deduplication, and balancing across domains. A larger but noisier corpus can actually hurt, because the model spends capacity fitting low-quality patterns.

The second lesson was about diversity. The first model was fairly strong on the distribution it saw, but brittle when you moved outside it. For the next generation we deliberately broadened the sources, including more structured data, more long-form material, and more examples that require reasoning across a whole document rather than just local prediction. That shift showed up clearly in downstream capability, more than the headline token count would suggest.

And the third point is that data and compute have to be matched. If you grow the data without growing training compute proportionally, you are just sampling it once and leaving value on the table. So the increase was planned together with the training budget rather than as an independent decision.

So if I had to summarize: yes, the data grew substantially, but I would assess the real gain as coming from quality and coverage. If we had simply scaled the first corpus by a large factor without those changes, I do not think we would have seen the same improvement.

r001.rationale: The response says the second generation involved more filtering and that quality and coverage mattered more than token count. It does not clearly explain how stricter filtering changes the first-generation baseline for measuring the data increase.

astra-6.text: I think the key is to distinguish the amount of data from the amount of useful information. Going from the first model to the next generation, you can collect much more data, but if it’s repetitive or low quality, the benefit may be limited. I would look at whether the additional data improves diversity and coverage, and whether those improvements translate into better model performance. So I wouldn’t assess the increase purely by its size; I’d assess what the model actually learns from it.

sol-6.1.text: I’d distinguish the amount of data we collected from the amount that actually helped the model. Increasing the volume gives us more coverage, but the value depends on quality, diversity, and how much repetition there is. So I wouldn’t assess the next generation just by how many times larger the dataset became. I’d look at whether that additional data translated into better generalization and more reliable performance. We haven’t established specific numbers here, so I wouldn’t put a multiplier on it.
